title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 211: The Wood Wide Web: Rethinking the Subterranean Forest
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 211 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Wood Wide Web: Rethinking the Subterranean Forest

Paragraph 1. For over a century, traditional forest science viewed trees as lone fighters competing fiercely for light, water, and nutrients. Whenever one tree captured moisture, experts assumed its neighbours suffered. Over the last thirty years, however, researchers have uncovered a very different picture beneath the forest floor. Hidden under fallen leaves lies an intricate underground web of mycorrhizal fungi linking trees of different ages and species into one connected community.

Paragraph 2. This underground partnership works through biological trade. Trees are experts at making carbon sugars from sunlight, yet their thick roots struggle to absorb minerals like phosphorus and nitrogen from packed soil. Conversely, mycorrhizal fungi grow microscopic threads called hyphae that reach into millions of tiny soil spaces, collecting water and vital nutrients. In return, trees supply up to forty percent of their sugars directly to the fungal network.

Paragraph 3. To watch resources travel across this living network, ecologist Dr. Suzanne Simard carried out a famous experiment in western Canada. Her team sealed branches of Douglas fir and paper birch trees inside airtight plastic bags and added special carbon markers. Tracking tools showed carbon moving in both directions through the fungi. In midsummer, sunlit birch trees shared extra carbon with shaded young firs; in autumn, when birch trees lost their leaves, evergreen firs sent carbon back.

Paragraph 4. Beyond sharing food, the fungal web carries early danger alerts. Eco-physiologist Dr. Kathryn Fahy tested how plants react when insects called aphids attack them. Connected healthy plants quickly produced defensive chemicals within twenty-four hours to drive pests away and attract helpful wasps. However, when Fahy cut the fungal threads between plants, nearby trees received no warnings and were left unprotected.

Paragraph 5. Ancient 'mother trees' sit at the heart of this forest network, connecting with hundreds of surrounding trees. Dr. Marcus Thorne discovered that mother trees recognise their own family, sending extra carbon to related young trees. Unfortunately, heavy logging and chemical sprays destroy this underground web. Simard now urges loggers to leave veteran hub trees standing so newly planted seedlings can join the established network and survive better.

q1.text: Traditional forestry a century ago believed trees regularly shared water and food equally.

steps: Đoạn 1: Khoa học lâm nghiệp truyền thống coi cây là những cá thể đơn độc cạnh tranh khốc liệt (lone fighters competing fiercely).

q2.text: Host trees pass a significant portion of their sugars to underground fungi.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...supply up to forty percent of their sugars directly to the fungal network."

q3.text: Dr. Suzanne Simard's Canadian forest experiment took fifteen years to finish.

steps: Đoạn 3: Chỉ nhắc địa điểm thí nghiệm ở tây Canada, không nói thời gian kéo dài 15 năm.

q4.text: Cutting fungal threads between plants still allowed distress signals to travel through the dirt.

steps: Đoạn 4: Khi cắt sợi nấm, các cây lân cận không nhận được cảnh báo (received no warnings).

q5.text: Leaving old hub trees uncut helps young planted trees survive more easily.

steps: Đoạn 5: Giữ lại cây mẹ giúp cây con kết nối mạng lưới và sống sót tốt hơn.
